title: Trump Is Making a Mess of Diego Garcia
gist: Grossman argues Trump's reversal on the 2025 UK-Mauritius Chagos treaty has frozen implementation, strained UK and Indian ties, and handed China a narrative win and an opening with Mauritius and other Indian Ocean states, even though the treaty would leave the Diego Garcia base under a 99-year paid lease.

insights.claim: Under the 2024 UK-Mauritius deal, formalized in May 2025, sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago transfers to Mauritius while US and British forces retain Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease with a 40-year extension option.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: The legal structure preserves base access, so the sovereignty transfer should not by itself change military operations.
insights.locator: After nearly two years of negotiations

insights.claim: Trump reversed from endorsing the deal to calling it 'an act of GREAT STUPIDITY' on Jan. 20, apparently driven by anger at European defense of Danish sovereignty over Greenland and objections from Kemi Badenoch relayed through Mike Johnson.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: US policy toward allies' territorial arrangements is being driven by linkage and personal channels, raising unpredictability.
insights.locator: But on Jan. 20, Trump abruptly reversed course.

insights.claim: The back-and-forth has stalled the deal: London suspended implementation in April and Mauritius has threatened legal action, with no easy off-ramp because Britain cannot move forward on the base without US consent.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Expect continued legal and diplomatic friction; resolution depends on Washington, not London.

insights.claim: Iran fired two ballistic missiles toward Diego Garcia in March, though neither struck the island, underscoring its value as a base for operations against Iran.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Confirms Diego Garcia as a strategic target in the Iran conflict; relevant to Indian Ocean military risk.

insights.claim: Trump's intervention reinforces China's narrative that Washington disregards small-state sovereignty and gives Indian Ocean states another reason to value Beijing as a strategic partner, an 'own goal' for the US.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: US overreach on Chagos could shift Indian Ocean alignments toward China and boost Chinese influence over Mauritius.
insights.quote: Washington has scored yet another own goal.

insights.claim: India backed Mauritian sovereignty and welcomed the treaty but also wants the US base on Diego Garcia secure against China, leaving New Delhi awkwardly balanced between Mauritius and its US partnership.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Adds friction to US-India ties already strained; watch New Delhi's language.

insights.claim: The treaty bars other militaries from the archipelago without British approval, but Washington and London worry Beijing could seek civilian or dual-use access, and enforcement depends on continued UK-Mauritius cooperation.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: A collapsed treaty weakens the safeguard against Chinese footholds, the very outcome Trump says he wants to prevent.
insights.locator: The Chagos treaty prohibits other military forces

insights.claim: Mauritius lacks the military capability to take control of the base even if it wanted to, so the transfer would not fundamentally alter base operations.
insights.speaker: Derek Grossman
insights.so_what: Undercuts the security case against the deal.
insights.locator: Even if Mauritius wanted to take control
